record.paper_title: Confinement of color: open problems and perspectives.
record.original_question: How important is the gauge-group center to the confinement mechanism, and what can be learned by comparing different gauge theories that share the same center or by studying confining gauge groups with no center, such as G_2? In particular, can direct comparisons across such theories determine whether center degrees of freedom, rather than some broader class of magnetic or topological excitations, are essential to confinement?

evidence.quote: An interesting recent development is the exploration of the role of the center in the process of confinement[23] to check the claim that vortices are the relevant excitations. In particular the gauge group G2 which has no center does confine color.

Direct investigation of the role of the center by comparison of different groups with the same center can provide useful information, as well as the study of confinement with gauge groups like G2 which have no center.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let G be a compact, simple Lie group, and consider four-dimensional Yang–Mills gauge theory with gauge group G, formulated either in the continuum or on a Euclidean lattice. The center Z(G) of G is widely believed to play a role in the confinement of static color charges: for example, in SU(N) gauge theory the center Z_N labels 't Hooft electric/magnetic flux sectors and the center-vortex mechanism attributes the asymptotic area law of the fundamental Wilson loop to the condensation of thin/thick vortices carrying flux in Z(G). However, the exceptional Lie group G_2 has trivial center, yet its pure gauge theory is known to exhibit a confining (linearly rising) intermediate-distance potential between static fundamental charges, with string breaking at large distances because the fundamental representation can be screened by gluons.

Make this precise as the following problem. Determine the role of the center Z(G) in the confinement mechanism of pure Yang–Mills theory by:

(a) giving a sharp criterion that distinguishes phenomena attributable specifically to center degrees of freedom from those attributable to a broader class of magnetic or topological excitations (monopoles, calorons, dyons, generalized vortices, etc.);

(b) using direct comparison of theories whose gauge groups share the same center (for instance SU(N) at different N, or SU(N) versus Sp(N) where their centers coincide) to test whether observables such as the string tension, its N-ality dependence, the spectrum of glueballs, and the deconfinement transition are controlled by Z(G) alone; and

(c) using gauge groups with trivial center such as G_2 (and related centerless or partially-centerless groups) to decide whether genuine center degrees of freedom are necessary for the existence of a confining intermediate-distance string and a sharp finite-temperature deconfinement transition, or whether all confinement phenomena present in the centerless case can already be explained by a non-center mechanism that also operates in SU(N).

The problem is to settle, on the basis of analytic argument and/or lattice evidence, whether center degrees of freedom are essential to the confinement mechanism of pure Yang–Mills theory, or whether they are merely a convenient bookkeeping device for a more general class of magnetic/topological excitations responsible for confinement in all compact simple gauge groups.
artifact.status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made: lattice studies of G_2 gauge theory (which has trivial center) demonstrate an intermediate-distance confining potential with string breaking at large distances, and there is a finite-temperature deconfinement transition. This is widely cited as evidence that strict center-vortex condensation is not necessary for confinement, while center degrees of freedom remain important in SU(N) for the asymptotic string tension and N-ality. However, no consensus mechanism unifying these observations has been established, and the precise role of the center versus broader magnetic/topological excitations remains an open conceptual problem actively discussed in the lattice and continuum literature.

status_evidence.title: Exceptional confinement in G(2) gauge theory
status_evidence.snippet: G(2) lattice gauge theories still confine without a center... center vortices should not be necessary to explain the absence of colored states
status_evidence.claim: Lattice G_2 gauge theory exhibits confinement despite trivial center, indicating center vortices are not strictly required.

status_evidence.title: Open issues in confinement, for the lattice and for center vortices
status_evidence.snippet: Open issues in confinement... center vortices
status_evidence.claim: The role of center vortices in confinement remains an open issue under active discussion.
